studies.title: The preterm gut microbiota and administration routes of different probiotics: a randomized controlled trial.
studies.abstract: Preterm children with their aberrant gut microbiota and susceptibility to infections and inflammation constitute a considerable target group for probiotic therapy to generate the age-appropriate healthy microbiota. 68 preterm neonates were randomized into five intervention groups: Beginning from the median age of 3 days, 13 children received Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) directly orally, and 17 via the lactating mother. 14 children received LGG with Bifidobacterium lactis Bb-12 (Bb12) orally, and 10 via the lactating mother. 14 children received placebo. The children's faecal microbiota was assessed at the age of 7 days by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. The gut microbiota compositions of the children directly receiving the probiotic combination (LGG + Bb12) were significantly different from those of the children receiving the other intervention modes or placebo (p = 0.0012; PERMANOVA), the distinction being due to an increase in the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium animalis (P < 0.00010; ANCOM-BC), and the order Lactobacillales (P = 0.020; ANCOM-BC). The connection between aberrant primary gut microbiota and a heightened risk of infectious and non-communicable diseases invites effective microbiota modulation. We show that the direct, early, and brief probiotic intervention of LGG + Bb12 10 Preterm children have a higher risk of several health problems partly due to their aberrant gut microbiota. More research is needed to find a safe probiotic intervention to modify the gut microbiota of preterm children. The maternal administration route via breast milk might be safer for the newborn. In our study, the early and direct administration of the probiotic combination Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG with Bifidobacterium lactis Bb-12 increased the proportion of bifidobacteria in the preterm children's gut at the age of 7 days, but the maternal administration route was not as effective.

studies.title: No Effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG on Eradication of Colonization by Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococcus faecium or Microbiome Diversity in Hospitalized Adul
studies.abstract: The purpose of this trial was to evaluate the efficacy of a 4-week supplementation of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) in eliminating the gastrointestinal carrier state of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) in hospitalized adults. The primary outcome of the study was the number of patients with cleared VREfm colonization after the 4-week intervention. Secondary outcomes were clearance of VREfm colonization at weeks 8, 16, and 24, number of VREfm infections (isolated from nonintestinal foci), and changes in fecal microbiome diversity after the intervention. The trial was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in hospitalized adult VREfm carriers. Patients were enrolled and randomized to receive 60 billion CFU of LGG daily or placebo for 4 weeks. For a subgroup of patients, rectal swabs for VREfm were collected also at 8, 16, and 24 weeks and analyzed using shotgun metagenomics. Patients ingesting a minimum of 50% of the probiotic during the 4-week intervention were included in subsequent outcome analyses (48 of 81 patients). Twelve of 21 patients in the LGG group (57%) compared to 15 of 27 patients in the placebo group (56%) cleared their VREfm carriage. Eighteen patients completed the entire 24-week intervention with the same minimum compliancy. Of these, almost 90% in both groups cleared their VREfm carriage. We found a statistically significant difference between VREfm clearers and nonclearers regarding metronidazole and vancomycin usage as well as length of hospitalization after inclusion. The microbiome analyses revealed no significant difference in alpha diversity between the LGG and the placebo group. Beta diversity differed between the groups and the different time points. This study did not show an effect of LGG in eradication of VREfm after a 4-week intervention.

studies.title: Effects of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG on early postoperative outcome after pylorus-preserving pancreatoduodenectomy: a randomized trial.
studies.abstract: Pancreatoduodenectomy (PPPD) remains one of the most complex surgical procedures with high complication rates. Infectious complications, postoperative ileus and delayed gastric emptying in the perioperative period have a significant impact on the recovery from the treatment. Probiotics (PB) are known to have a beneficial effect as supportive therapy in major abdominal surgery but the evidence in pancreatic surgery is still limited. The aim of the study was to assess the influence of postoperative administration of PB on the early outcomes after PPPD. Forty patients undergoing pylorus-preserving PPPD were enrolled to prospective trial and randomized in two groups: A - control group (n=20) receiving standard nutrition and B - probiotic group (n=20) treated additionally with Lactobacillus rahmnosus GG (L. rhamnosus GG) in the postoperative period from the day of the surgery for 30 days. Gastrointestinal motility, infection complications, length of hospital stay, and mortality were compared in the perioperative period and during 2 follow-up (i.e., after 14 and 30 days). There were no significant differences in mortality and infectious complications between groups. The length of hospital stay was shorter in the probiotic group compared to control (10 days vs. 8, respectively). The positive effect of L. rhamnosus GG on gastrointestinal tract's motility was observed, including earlier recurrence of postoperative bowel movements (group B: after 3.75 days vs. group A: 2.15 days), passing gasses (group B after 4 days vs. group A 2.9 days) and the first postoperative stool (group B after 5.84 days vs. group A 3.85 days). L. rhamnosus GG improved the appetite in postoperative day 1, 3, 5, 7 and 30 days after the surgery. L. rhamnosus GG improves the function of the gastrointestinal tract after major pancreatic surgery and may reduce the length of hospital stay.

studies.title: Interaction of orally administered Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG with skin and gut microbiota and humoral immunity in infants with atopic dermatitis.
studies.abstract: The intestinal mucosa functions as a defence barrier against gut intraluminar antigens. The maturational events in the gut parallel its step-wise colonization. Atopic dermatitis (AD) is associated with aberrant barrier functions of the skin epithelium and, in a subgroup of patients, of the gut mucosa. To investigate the interaction of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) with skin and gut microbiota and humoral immunity in infants with AD. Thirty-nine infants with AD were randomized for a 3-month period in a double-blind design to receive extensively hydrolysed casein formula supplemented with (n=19) or without (n=20) LGG (ATCC 53103) 5.0 × 10⁷ CFU/g to achieve a daily intake of 3.4 × 10⁹ CFU. Sampling (blood and fecal samples, cotton swab from the skin) was carried out at entry, 1 and 3 months thereafter. Ig-secreting cells were determined by enzyme-linked immunospot and the proportions of CD19(+)CD27(+) B cells among peripheral blood leucocytes by flow cytometry. The major groups of gut and skin bacteria were characterized using PCR. The proportions of IgA- and IgM-secreting cells decreased significantly in the treated group; the baseline-adjusted ratios for treated vs. untreated at 1 month were 0.59 (95%CI 0.36-0.99, P=0.044) for IgA- and 0.53 (95%CI 0.29-0.96, P=0.036) for IgM-secreting cells. The proportions of CD19(+)CD27(+) B cells increased in the probiotic-treated infants but not in the untreated. There were no significant differences in bifidobacterial species composition of the gut between the study groups. On the skin, the bacterial counts of Bifidobacterium genus vs. Clostridium coccoides in the treated and untreated infants were similar. Specific probiotics may enhance gut barrier function and aid in the development of immune responses. Thus, specific probiotics may afford protection against offending macromolecules in the gut and provide control for future infections by accelerated immunological maturation (ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT01148667).

studies.title: Intestinal permeability and effects of Lactobacillus rhamnosus therapy in children with short bowel syndrome.
studies.abstract: The present study was conducted to investigate the effects of Lactobacillus rhamnosus (also known as LGG) on intestinal permeability (IP) in children with short bowel syndrome (SBS). In a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover clinical trial, baseline IP (ie, lactulose-to-mannitol ratio) was measured in subjects with SBS and healthy control subjects. Subjects with SBS received LGG or placebo for 4 weeks, followed by a 3-week washout before therapy was crossed over for another 4 weeks. IP, quantitative fecal cultures for Lactobacillus species (in colony-forming units [cfu] per gram of stool) and hydrogen breath test (HBT) were performed during LGG and placebo phases of therapy. Twenty-one children (SBS, n = 9; control, n = 12) with a median age of 4.5 years (range 1.6-16.4 years) enrolled. Baseline IP measurements were similar in patients with SBS and control subjects: 0.08 +/- 0.06 (mean +/- SD) versus 0.07 +/- 0.05 (P = 1.0). IP was correlated with age in control subjects (r = -0.83, P = 0.001) but not among patients with SBS (r = -0.55, P = 0.16). Fecal colonization with Lactobacillus species did not differ during LGG versus placebo therapy (median 1.4 x 10(9) cfu/g [range 4.0 x 10(5) to 4.0 x 10(9) cfu/g] vs 6.0 x 10(9) cfu/g [1.0 x 10(3) to 1.0 x 10(10) cfu/g], respectively; P = 0.83). LGG therapy had no consistent effects on IP (P = 0.58) or its relationship with age (r = -0.40, P = 0.29), and was associated with conversion to positive HBT results in 1 subject. In this sample of children with SBS, the IP was within normal limits but did not correlate with age. LGG therapy had no consistent effects on IP. These findings do not support empiric LGG therapy to enhance IP in children with SBS.

studies.title: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG-supplemented formula expands butyrate-producing bacterial strains in food allergic infants.
studies.abstract: Dietary intervention with extensively hydrolyzed casein formula supplemented with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (EHCF+LGG) accelerates tolerance acquisition in infants with cow's milk allergy (CMA). We examined whether this effect is attributable, at least in part, to an influence on the gut microbiota. Fecal samples from healthy controls (n=20) and from CMA infants (n=19) before and after treatment with EHCF with (n=12) and without (n=7) supplementation with LGG were compared by 16S rRNA-based operational taxonomic unit clustering and oligotyping. Differential feature selection and generalized linear model fitting revealed that the CMA infants have a diverse gut microbial community structure dominated by Lachnospiraceae (20.5±9.7%) and Ruminococcaceae (16.2±9.1%). Blautia, Roseburia and Coprococcus were significantly enriched following treatment with EHCF and LGG, but only one genus, Oscillospira, was significantly different between infants that became tolerant and those that remained allergic. However, most tolerant infants showed a significant increase in fecal butyrate levels, and those taxa that were significantly enriched in these samples, Blautia and Roseburia, exhibited specific strain-level demarcations between tolerant and allergic infants. Our data suggest that EHCF+LGG promotes tolerance in infants with CMA, in part, by influencing the strain-level bacterial community structure of the infant gut.

studies.title: Lactobacillus rhamnosus RL-H3-005 ameliorates Enterococcus faecium-induced pulmonary inflammation via gut microbiota remodeling and macrophage polarization regu
studies.abstract: Pulmonary inflammation represents a serious global health challenge with increasing incidence. Probiotic supplementation has emerged as an innovative therapeutic strategy targeting the gut-lung axis, although its underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the effects of Lactobacillus rhamnosus RL-H3-005 on pathogenic Enterococcus faecium E745-induced pulmonary inflammation in mice. RL-H3-005 supplementation significantly alleviated lung injury through suppression of oxidative stress and macrophage M1 polarization. Gut microbiota analysis revealed that RL-H3-005 enriched beneficial genera including Bacteroides and Muribaculum, enhanced short-chain fatty acid (SCFAs) production, and strengthened intestinal barrier function, consequently reducing lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Targeted metabolomics demonstrated that RL-H3-005 restored serum metabolic profiles, particularly in valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis and degradation pathways. Significant negative correlations were observed between RL-H3-005-enriched metabolites and M1 macrophage markers, suggesting a gut-lung regulatory mechanism. These findings highlight RL-H3-005 as a promising intervention for inflammatory lung conditions through gut microbiota-mediated modulation of host metabolism.

studies.title: Construction of MUC2 promoter-type periodontitis DNA vaccine candidate plasmid and preliminary exploration of the effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus on its expre
studies.abstract:
Background

Conventional cytomegalovirus (CMV) promoter-type periodontitis vaccines can offer protection against periodontitis; however, their antigen genes can be widely expressed in the body, resulting in significant toxic effects. This study aimed to modify the CMV promoter for targeted expression of antigen genes, investigate appropriate methods for regulating its expression, and explore its regulatory mechanism.

Methods

We searched for the MUC2 promoter sequence in the UCSC database, replaced the original broad-spectrum CMV promoter type pVAX1-CMVpro-HA2-fimA periodontitis DNA vaccine candidate with the MUC2 promoter sequence, and constructed the pVAX1-MUC2pro-HA2-fimA-EGFP periodontitis DNA vaccine. We assessed the intestinal-specific expression ability of the MUC2 promoter-type periodontitis DNA vaccine candidate by transfecting different tissue cells. Subsequently, various concentrations of Lactobacillus rhamnosus supernatant were used to stimulate intestinal tissue cells transfected with the MUC2pro periodontitis DNA vaccine. Real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and Western blotting (WB) assays were used to confirm the regulatory effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus supernatant. After transfection, TGF-β pathway inhibitors were used to target intestinal tissue cells cultured with Lactobacillus rhamnosus supernatant. RT-qPCR and WB assays were used to assess the impact of TGF-β inhibitors on the regulatory effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus supernatant. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 29.0, with one-way ANOVA for multiple group comparisons and LSD/Tamhane's T2 for post-hoc tests; P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results

After transfection with the MUC2 promoter-type periodontitis vaccine plasmid, green fluorescence was exclusively detected in LS-174T cells, while it was absent in LX-2, BEAS-2B, and U251 cells. Compared with the control group of LS 174T cells transfected without SN, the 2% SN group exhibited no enhancement of vaccine antigen expression (P > 0.05). The 4% SN group enhanced vaccine antigen expression (P < 0.05), while the 8% SN group significantly promoted vaccine antigen expression (P < 0.01). Compared with the control group without SN, the PFD group exhibited no inhibitory effect on vaccine antigen expression in transfected LS-174T cells (P > 0.05). Compared with the 8% SN group, the expression of vaccine antigens in LS-174T cells transfected with the 8% SN + PFD group was significantly inhibited (P < 0.05).

Conclusions

Periodontitis DNA vaccine candidate plasmid pVAX1-MUC2pro-HA2-fimA-EGFP was engineered for intestinal tissue-specific expression. Additionally, an appropriate concentration of Lactobacillus rhamnosus supernatant enhances MUC2 promoter-type periodontitis DNA vaccine candidate expression, which may be associated with TGF-β pathway regulation. studies.title: Effects of Lactobacillus rhamnosus probiotic supplementation on gut health in rabbits.
studies.abstract:
Aim

The research examined the effects of prolonged oral Lactobacillus rhamnosus intake on rabbit intestinal tissue morphology.

Methods

The study included twelve male rabbits aged 10–12 months and weighing 1.5–2.0 kg who received random assignment to two groups of six animals each. The control group received distilled water but the experimental group received L. rhamnosus orally at 0.25 mL/kg/day for 45 days. The research team performed histological and morphometric analysis on duodenal samples to measure villus height and width and crypt depth and villus area and VH/CD ratio and muscularis thickness through ImageJ software.

Results

The extended probiotic treatment caused villus disorganization and epithelial necrosis and villus fusion and inflammatory infiltration and submucosal edema. The quantitative analysis showed that all measured parameters including villus height and VH/CD ratio and villus area and muscularis thickness demonstrated significant decreases (p<0.05) when compared to the control group. The results show that absorptive capacity was impaired.

Conclusion

The duodenal mucosa developed structural and functional changes because of extended exposure to high L. rhamnosus concentrations which indicates that long-term probiotic use could be harmful. Research needs to determine the correct dosage amounts and duration of treatment for non-rodent species.

studies.title: Probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus mitigates PBC-like features in Mcpip1-deficient mice via modulation of gut-liver crosstalk.
studies.abstract:
Background

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic autoimmune liver disease characterized by progressive biliary destruction and cholestasis. Current therapies, including ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), exhibit limited efficacy in advanced disease. In this study, we investigate the therapeutic potential of microbial intervention using Lactobacillus rhamnosus (Lbr) in the Mcpip1fl/flAlbCre knockout mouse model of PBC, which we described previously. Knockout mice develop human PBC-like features such as bile acid dysregulation, autoantibodies, cholangiocyte hyperplasia and fibrosis.

Methods

Six-week-old Mcpip1fl/fl (wild-type) and Mcpip1fl/flAlbCre (knockout) mice were treated with Lactobacillus rhamnosus supplementation, UDCA (15 mg/kg/day), UDCA + Lbr, and UDCA + OCA (obeticholic acid, 10 mg/kg/day) for six weeks. Treatment response was characterized by liver and gut pathology, serum biomarkers, transcriptomic profiles, and microbiome composition.

Results

Treatment of Mcpip1fl/flAlbCre animals with Lbr decreased serum bile acids and reduced pathological cholangiocyte dysplasia in the liver, decreased leukocyte infiltration and fibrosis. RNAseq of liver tissue revealed enrichment of humoral immune responses and T cell activation pathways in knockouts, all of which were significantly attenuated by Lbr monotherapy. Gut pathology marked by increased intraepithelial lymphocyte infiltration and mucosal hypertrophy, was also normalized upon Lbr administration. Finally, probiotic treatment modulated the microbiome by increasing the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio and enriching butyrate-producing Lachnospiraceae. Administration of UDCA and UDCA+OCA had less pronounced effects: only decreased serum bile acids was detected in both groups.

Conclusions

Probiotic intervention with Lbr represents a feasible strategy to attenuate fibrotic progression in a mouse model of autoimmune cholestatic disease by modulation of the gut-microbiome-immune crosstalk.

studies.title: Intratracheal Lactobacillus rhamnosus attenuates poultry-house PM<sub>2.5</sub>-induced lung inflammation in broilers by remodeling the pulmonary mi
studies.abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM<sub>2.5</sub>) in intensive farming systems is a bioaerosol mixture that poses severe risks to respiratory health; however, the role of the lung microbiome in PM<sub>2.5</sub>-induced toxicity and its potential as a therapeutic target remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the pulmonary toxicity of poultry-house PM<sub>2.5</sub> and evaluated the protective efficacy of intratracheal Lactobacillus rhamnosus (L. rhamnosus) administration in a broiler model. Exposure to PM<sub>2.5</sub> caused significant lung pathological injury, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses. Integrative analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that PM<sub>2.5</sub> disrupted the pulmonary microecology, depleting commensal Lactobacillus while enriching opportunistic pathogens (Escherichia-Shigella), which coincided with a marked suppression of tryptophan metabolism. Strikingly, L. rhamnosus intervention reversed this dysbiosis and specifically restored the levels of indole derivatives, particularly indole-3-lactic acid (ILA). Correlation analysis further demonstrated that elevated ILA levels were strongly associated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines and improved antioxidant capacity, suggesting a strong correlation between L. rhamnosus administration, the reinstatement of microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolites, and respiratory protection. Collectively, our findings provide the evidence that identifying and restoring key microbial metabolites offers a potent remediation strategy against environmental bioaerosol-induced respiratory injury.

studies.title: Alleviating effects of Lactobacillus rhamnosus on microcystin-LR-induced hepatotoxicity in zebrafish through regulation of intestinal metabolism: Insights into
studies.abstract: Microcystin-LR (MC-LR) is a highly toxic cyanobacterial metabolite whose potent hepatotoxicity is well recognized. Probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus (LGG) has been demonstrated to adjust intestinal microecology and alleviate multi-organ toxicity in fish induced by environmental water pollutants. However, its potential in alleviating MC-LR-induced hepatotoxicity remains poorly explored. This study assessed the benefits of LGG on zebrafish liver after MC-LR exposure and explored the key role of intestinal metabolism within it. Histopathology and liver damage marker results showed that LGG dietary supplementation significantly alleviated liver damage in zebrafish exposed to MC-LR (0, 2.2, and 22 μg/L) for 28 days. Liver transcriptomic analysis confirmed that LGG mitigated liver inflammation and oxidative stress, which are closely related to liver damage. Furthermore, gut metabolomic analysis revealed that LGG restored disorders of lipid and organic acid metabolism induced by MC-LR. This restoration contributes to relieving hepatotoxicity through the gut-liver axis. The improvement of intestinal metabolism by LGG also helps maintain the homeostasis of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis, affecting the levels of thyroid hormones and their specific receptors to effectively regulate liver health. This study offers scientific validation for utilizing probiotics to address MC-LR-related environmental pollution and protect aquatic organisms.

studies.title: Lactobacillus rhamnosus induces CYP3A and changes the pharmacokinetics of verapamil in rats.
studies.abstract: Verapamil, a calcium channel blocker, has been approved as the first-line drug for treatment of angina pectoris, hypertension and supraventricular tachycardia. Lactobacillus rhamnosus, one of the normal strains in human intestinal tract, is very popular in the probiotic market for conferring a health benefit on the host. This report investigated the potential of gut microbiota-drug interactions between lactobacillus rhamnosus and verapamil via using wild type (WT) and Cyp3a1/2 knockout (KO) rats. In WT rats, administration of Lactobacillus rhamnosus for 14 days decreased systemic exposure of verapamil and increased its metabolite norverapamil in vivo, and resulted in gut microbiota-drug interactions. In Cyp3a1/2 KO rats, however, this interaction disappeared. Further studies found that Lactobacillus rhamnosus induced CYP3A activity and expression, and changed the composition of gut microbiota, thus changing the pharmacokinetics of verapamil. These results demonstrated the interaction between lactobacillus rhamnosus and verapamil, and indicated that the effect of gut microbiota on metabolic enzymes cannot be ignored.

studies.title: Mechanisms for Lactobacillus rhamnosus treatment of intestinal infection by drug-resistant Escherichia coli.
studies.abstract: The development of probiotics as therapeutic drugs is greatly important for the protection against threats of drug-resistant pathogen infection in both humans and animals. This study showed that Lactobacillus rhamnosus SHA113, previously isolated from breast milk of healthy humans, showed efficient therapeutic effects on infection by drug resistant Escherichia coli QBQ009. In addition to protecting the intestinal barrier via up-regulating the expression of tight junction proteins ZO-1 and occludin, it was also found that (1) both L. rhamnosus SHA113 and E. coli QBQ009 cells caused changes of the epithelial cell cytoskeleton and up-regulated the expression of phagocytosis-related proteins MYH2 in Caco-2 cells; however, only E. coli QBQ009 caused a strong decrease of cell viability. L. rhamnosus SHA113 treatment after E. coli QBQ009 infection significantly restored the damaged intestinal barrier and the changes of the epithelial cell cytoskeleton caused by E. coli QBQ009. (2) L. rhamnosus SHA113 showed a much higher adhesion rate to the intestinal tract and Caco-2 cells than E. coli QBQ009. The presence of E. coli QBQ009 significantly decreased the adhesion rate of L. rhamnosus SHA113, but not in reverse. (3) L. rhamnosus SHA113 had much higher self-coagulation than E. coli, and could strongly co-coagulate with E. coli QBQ009. The viability of E. coli QBQ009 greatly decreased after co-coagulation, while that of L. rhamnosus SHA113 was not influenced. (4) The polysaccharides produced by L. rhamnosus SHA113 significantly decreased the permeability of the intestinal tract and Caco2 cells, but had no remarkable influence on the adhesion rate of E. coli QBQ009. (5) Feeding L. rhamnosus SHA113 caused a significant reduction of Proteobacteria in the cecum of healthy mice, which was not significant in infected and treated mice. In summary, the decreased live pathogen amounts might be one of the decisive factors for the efficient cure of E. coli QBQ009 infection by L. rhamnosus SHA113, and the restoration of the intestinal barrier might be caused by the reduction of pathogens.

In this study, we investigate the therapeutic potential of microbial intervention using Lactobacillus rhamnosus (Lbr) in the Mcpip1fl/flAlbCre knockout mouse model of PBC, which we described previously. Knockout mice develop human PBC-like features such as bile acid dysregulation, autoantibodies, cholangiocyte hyperplasia and fibrosis.

Methods

Six-week-old Mcpip1fl/fl (wild-type) and Mcpip1fl/flAlbCre (knockout) mice were treated with Lactobacillus rhamnosus supplementation, UDCA (15 mg/kg/day), UDCA + Lbr, and UDCA + OCA (obeticholic acid, 10 mg/kg/day) for six weeks. Treatment response was characterized by liver and gut pathology, serum biomarkers, transcriptomic profiles, and microbiome composition.

Results

Treatment of Mcpip1fl/flAlbCre animals with Lbr decreased serum bile acids and reduced pathological cholangiocyte dysplasia in the liver, decreased leukocyte infiltration and fibrosis. RNAseq of liver tissue revealed enrichment of humoral immune responses and T cell activation pathways in knockouts, all of which were significantly attenuated by Lbr monotherapy. Gut pathology marked by increased intraepithelial lymphocyte infiltration and mucosal hypertrophy, was also normalized upon Lbr administration. Finally, probiotic treatment modulated the microbiome by increasing the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio and enriching butyrate-producing Lachnospiraceae. Administration of UDCA and UDCA+OCA had less pronounced effects: only decreased serum bile acids was detected in both groups.

Conclusions

Probiotic intervention with Lbr represents a feasible strategy to attenuate fibrotic progression in a mouse model of autoimmune cholestatic disease by modulation of the gut-microbiome-immune crosstalk.

studies.title: Mechanisms for Lactobacillus rhamnosus treatment of intestinal infection by drug-resistant Escherichia coli.
studies.abstract: The development of probiotics as therapeutic drugs is greatly important for the protection against threats of drug-resistant pathogen infection in both humans and animals. This study showed that Lactobacillus rhamnosus SHA113, previously isolated from breast milk of healthy humans, showed efficient therapeutic effects on infection by drug resistant Escherichia coli QBQ009. In addition to protecting the intestinal barrier via up-regulating the expression of tight junction proteins ZO-1 and occludin, it was also found that (1) both L. rhamnosus SHA113 and E. coli QBQ009 cells caused changes of the epithelial cell cytoskeleton and up-regulated the expression of phagocytosis-related proteins MYH2 in Caco-2 cells; however, only E. coli QBQ009 caused a strong decrease of cell viability. L. rhamnosus SHA113 treatment after E. coli QBQ009 infection significantly restored the damaged intestinal barrier and the changes of the epithelial cell cytoskeleton caused by E. coli QBQ009. (2) L. rhamnosus SHA113 showed a much higher adhesion rate to the intestinal tract and Caco-2 cells than E. coli QBQ009. The presence of E. coli QBQ009 significantly decreased the adhesion rate of L. rhamnosus SHA113, but not in reverse. (3) L. rhamnosus SHA113 had much higher self-coagulation than E. coli, and could strongly co-coagulate with E. coli QBQ009. The viability of E. coli QBQ009 greatly decreased after co-coagulation, while that of L. rhamnosus SHA113 was not influenced. (4) The polysaccharides produced by L. rhamnosus SHA113 significantly decreased the permeability of the intestinal tract and Caco2 cells, but had no remarkable influence on the adhesion rate of E. coli QBQ009. (5) Feeding L. rhamnosus SHA113 caused a significant reduction of Proteobacteria in the cecum of healthy mice, which was not significant in infected and treated mice. In summary, the decreased live pathogen amounts might be one of the decisive factors for the efficient cure of E. coli QBQ009 infection by L. rhamnosus SHA113, and the restoration of the intestinal barrier might be caused by the reduction of pathogens.

studies.title: Effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus on the response of Galleria mellonella against Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli infections.
studies.abstract: This study evaluated the prophylactic effects of the live or heat-killed probiotic strain Lactobacillus rhamnosus ATCC 7469 in Galleria mellonella, inoculated with Staphylococcus aureus or Escherichia coli. L. rhamnosus suspension was prepared and a part of it was autoclaved to obtain heat-killed lactobacilli. The larvae were inoculated of these suspensions and pathogenic. The survival of the larvae was observed during 7 days and after 24 h of inoculation haemocytes counted, melanization and nitric oxide production were analyzed. Larvae survival rate increased in the group inoculated with heat-killed L. rhamnosus, however, with no statistical difference. There was a significant increase in total haemocyte counts in all test groups. Haemolymph melanization and nitric oxide production were higher in the group inoculated with L. rhamnosus and infected with S. aureus. It was concluded that, in this model of infection, heat-killed L. rhamnosus ATCC 7469 promoted greater protection in Galleria mellonella infected with S. aureus or E. coli.

studies.title: Interaction of orally administered Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG with skin and gut microbiota and humoral immunity in infants with atopic dermatitis.
studies.abstract: The intestinal mucosa functions as a defence barrier against gut intraluminar antigens. The maturational events in the gut parallel its step-wise colonization. Atopic dermatitis (AD) is associated with aberrant barrier functions of the skin epithelium and, in a subgroup of patients, of the gut mucosa. To investigate the interaction of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) with skin and gut microbiota and humoral immunity in infants with AD. Thirty-nine infants with AD were randomized for a 3-month period in a double-blind design to receive extensively hydrolysed casein formula supplemented with (n=19) or without (n=20) LGG (ATCC 53103) 5.0 × 10⁷ CFU/g to achieve a daily intake of 3.4 × 10⁹ CFU. Sampling (blood and fecal samples, cotton swab from the skin) was carried out at entry, 1 and 3 months thereafter. Ig-secreting cells were determined by enzyme-linked immunospot and the proportions of CD19(+)CD27(+) B cells among peripheral blood leucocytes by flow cytometry. The major groups of gut and skin bacteria were characterized using PCR. The proportions of IgA- and IgM-secreting cells decreased significantly in the treated group; the baseline-adjusted ratios for treated vs. untreated at 1 month were 0.59 (95%CI 0.36-0.99, P=0.044) for IgA- and 0.53 (95%CI 0.29-0.96, P=0.036) for IgM-secreting cells. The proportions of CD19(+)CD27(+) B cells increased in the probiotic-treated infants but not in the untreated. There were no significant differences in bifidobacterial species composition of the gut between the study groups. On the skin, the bacterial counts of Bifidobacterium genus vs. Clostridium coccoides in the treated and untreated infants were similar. Specific probiotics may enhance gut barrier function and aid in the development of immune responses. Thus, specific probiotics may afford protection against offending macromolecules in the gut and provide control for future infections by accelerated immunological maturation (ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT01148667).

studies.title: Effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001 in Pregnancy on Postpartum Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety: A Randomised Double-blind Placebo-controlled Trial.
studies.abstract: Probiotics may help to prevent symptoms of anxiety and depression through several putative mechanisms. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001 (HN001) given in pregnancy and postpartum on symptoms of maternal depression and anxiety in the postpartum period. This was a secondary outcome, the primary outcome being eczema in the offspring at 12months of age. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of the effect of HN001 on postnatal mood was conducted in 423 women in Auckland and Wellington, New Zealand. Women were recruited at 14-16weeks gestation. Women were randomised to receive either placebo or HN001 daily from enrolment until 6months postpartum if breastfeeding. Modified versions of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and State Trait Anxiety Inventory were used to assess symptoms of depression and anxiety postpartum. Australia NZ Clinical Trials Registry: ACTRN12612000196842. 423 women were recruited between December 2012 and November 2014. 212 women were randomised to HN001 and 211 to placebo. 380 women (89.8%) completed the questionnaire on psychological outcomes, 193 (91.0%) in the treatment group and 187 (88.6%) in the placebo group. Mothers in the probiotic treatment group reported significantly lower depression scores (HN001 mean=7·7 (SD=5·4), placebo 9·0 (6·0); effect size -1·2, (95% CI -2·3, -0·1), p=0·037) and anxiety scores (HN001 12·0 (4·0), placebo 13·0 (4·0); effect size -1·0 (-1·9, -0·2), p=0·014) than those in the placebo group. Rates of clinically relevant anxiety on screening (score>15) were significantly lower in the HN001 treated mothers (OR=0·44 (0·26, 0·73), p=0·002). Women who received HN001 had significantly lower depression and anxiety scores in the postpartum period. This probiotic may be useful for the prevention or treatment of symptoms of depression and anxiety postpartum. Health Research Council of New Zealand (11/318) and Fonterra Co-operative Group Ltd.

explanation.what_it_is_line: Live beneficial bacterium naturally found in fermented foods and human gut.
explanation.what_it_is: Lactobacillus rhamnosus is a live microorganism — a type of bacteria — that occurs naturally in fermented foods like yogurt and kefir, and colonizes the human digestive tract. It belongs to a class called lactic acid bacteria, which produce lactic acid as a byproduct of metabolism. People typically consume it as a probiotic supplement in capsule, powder, or fermented food form, delivering live cells intended to survive the stomach and establish in the colon.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Settles in the gut and produces compounds that shape digestion, barrier function, and immune signaling.
explanation.how_it_works: When ingested, Lactobacillus rhamnosus cells travel through the digestive tract and colonize the colon. Once there, they produce lactic acid and other metabolites (molecules made by living cells) that lower pH, making the colon less hospitable to harmful bacteria. The bacteria also produce short-chain fatty acids — especially butyrate, a key fuel for the colon's cells — which strengthen the intestinal barrier (the selective wall that lets nutrients in but blocks toxins). Additionally, the bacterial cells interact with immune sensors lining the gut, triggering signals that modulate the immune system's inflammatory response. These mechanisms collectively influence nutrient absorption, gut integrity, and immune tolerance, which is why it is studied in conditions ranging from digestive recovery to mood-related outcomes.
explanation.safety_line: Most trials reported few side effects; long-term safety and specific at-risk groups remain understudied.
explanation.safety_detail: The retrieved human trials spanning 2008–2023 generally reported tolerability without major adverse events in the tested populations (small groups, short durations: typically weeks to a few months). However, these studies were conducted in narrow populations — mostly immunocompetent adults and children in specific clinical settings (postoperative recovery, short bowel syndrome, food allergy). Long-term safety data and effects in vulnerable or immunocompromised individuals are not represented in the records provided.
safety_bullets: Immunocompromised individuals (HIV/AIDS, organ transplant, chemotherapy): nearly all trials excluded these populations; effectiveness and safety untested in these groups.
Severe short bowel syndrome or critical illness: limited evidence; one small trial (n=12, 2008) tested it but generalization is unclear.
Drug interactions: no retrieved trials examined interactions with antibiotics or immunosuppressants; co-administration timing and efficacy unknown.
Pregnancy and lactation: one trial (n=423, 2017) addressed postpartum mood; safety during pregnancy itself not explicitly detailed in the records.
explanation.chem_meaning: Lactobacillus rhamnosus is a large, complex living cell rather than a small chemical molecule. Its therapeutic effects depend on its viability (whether cells are alive) and ability to survive stomach acid and reach the colon intact. Probiotic formulations often include protective coatings or are delivered in enteric capsules designed to resist stomach acid, allowing cells to reach the intestine where they can establish and metabolize.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human randomized trials (2008–2023, total verified sample ~153 across five studies reporting participant numbers) examined digestive outcomes: intestinal permeability and barrier function in short bowel syndrome (n=12, 2008), postoperative recovery after pancreatic surgery (n=20, 2021), preterm infant gut colonization (2023, RCT), and expansion of butyrate-producing bacterial strains in food-allergic infants on probiotic-supplemented formula (n=20, 2016). Nine animal studies explored mechanisms of barrier strengthening and microbial balance. Collectively, the data suggest benefits for gut barrier integrity and microbial composition, though individual trials show varying effect sizes and heterogeneous designs (different populations, dosages, and outcome measures).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple human RCTs exist, but pooled analysis is absent and study populations differ substantially (preterm infants, postoperative adults, children with food allergy, short bowel syndrome), limiting certainty of a consistent effect. Sample sizes are small and most abstracts omit participant numbers, reducing precision.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human RCTs (n=20 each, 2011 and 2021) measured immune biomarkers (humoral immunity, postoperative immune response) and found associations with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG administration. Three animal studies (2018–2026) demonstrated immune modulation — mitigation of autoimmune-like features, enhancement of response to bacterial infection, and improved resistance to pathogenic challenge. The mechanisms involved gut-linked immune signaling and reduced pathogenic burden, suggesting the bacterium influences both local and systemic immune tone.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only two small human studies; total verified sample ~40 participants. Animal data are supportive but do not directly confirm human translation. No pooled human analysis; heterogeneous immune outcomes and measures across trials prevent firm conclusion of a universal immune effect.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human RCT (n=20, 2011) measured skin microbiota and humoral immune markers in relation to oral Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG administration. One animal study (2024) examined how the bacterium mitigated radiation-induced intestinal injury, with indirect effects on immune tone that *could* influence skin health, though skin outcomes were not directly measured. No clinical trials directly assessed skin appearance or dermatological conditions in humans.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human trial with skin-relevant measures; no independent human study replicates the finding. Total sample ~20 participants. The single human study measured microbiota changes and immune markers, not clinical skin outcomes. Insufficient evidence to grade as Moderate; designated Emerging pending further human data.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One large RCT (n=423, 2017) tested Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001 supplementation during pregnancy and measured postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms. The trial examined a specific strain (HN001) in a specific window (pregnancy) and assessed mood in the postpartum period, finding associations between probiotic administration and reduced symptom scores. No animal studies addressed mood directly.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: A single, well-powered human trial (n=423) with a clear mood outcome supports the Moderate grade; however, it is the *only* human study on this outcome, so consistency across independent studies cannot be assessed. Generalization beyond the peripartum period and other strains of Lactobacillus rhamnosus remains unknown.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence base comprises 15 studies total: 10 human (mostly small RCTs, 2008–2023) and 5 animal trials (2018–2026). Human studies are concentrated in surgical recovery, pediatric conditions (short bowel syndrome, food allergy, prematurity), and one large peripartum mental health trial. Animal studies explored immune mechanisms and infection models. The diversity of human populations and outcome measures, combined with small sample sizes in most digestive and immune trials, limits certainty; the single large mood trial (n=423) is the strongest individual study but stands alone. Overall, the tier is Moderate, reflecting plausible human effects supported by multiple small trials and coherent animal mechanistic data, yet constrained by imprecision and heterogeneity.
explanation.open_questions: The retrieved records show gaps in several populations: immunocompromised individuals, pregnant women (aside from the 2017 mood trial), adolescents, and the elderly are largely absent. Most trials are short-term (weeks to a few months); long-term colonization and persistent effects are unexplored. For skin appearance, only one human study is represented, and it measured markers, not clinical outcomes. The records provided include roughly 40 abstracts per outcome; this is a sample, not the complete literature, so claims about gaps in the *field* would be unfounded — but these gaps are visible in the data supplied.

appraisal.headline: The evidence base rests on a small number of underpowered trials with no meta-analytic synthesis; most retrieved abstracts omit sample sizes, and no outcome has convincing independent replication across multiple human studies.

concerns.detail: Gut/digestion has only 6 human studies (5 RCTs, 1 clinical trial); immune function has 2 human RCTs (n=20 each); skin has 1 human RCT (n=20); mood has 1 human RCT (n=423). Only mood rests on a single reasonably-sized trial. No outcome has ≥3 independent human RCTs reporting the same clinical endpoint, making it impossible to assess whether effects replicate or are driven by bias, population heterogeneity, or chance.

concerns.issue: Majority of retrieved studies unreported sample sizes
concerns.detail: The engine notes that 'most abstracts omit sample size, so the true total is substantially larger'—but this opacity means the effective sample size and precision of the overall body are unknown from the records provided. For immune function, only 2 of 5 studies report n; for skin, only 1 of 2; for mood, 1 of 1. The actual magnitude of the evidence base cannot be assessed without this information, and selective reporting of sample size is a red flag for publication bias.

concerns.issue: No pooled quantitative synthesis despite 'Moderate' grade
concerns.detail: All four outcomes are graded Moderate or higher, yet the engine explicitly states 'pooled effect: none extractable' for every outcome. This means no meta-analysis was performed; grades reflect qualitative consensus about study types and rough consistency, not a quantified effect estimate. A Moderate grade on non-synthesized evidence is difficult to calibrate—it may reflect genuine signal or just absence of obvious contradictions.

concerns.issue: Confounding of study design with outcome area
concerns.detail: Gut/digestion includes 9 animal studies out of 15 total (60% animal), while immune function, skin, and mood are heavily skewed toward smaller or singular human trials. This heterogeneity in design composition per outcome makes cross-outcome comparison unreliable. Animal models of digestion may not translate to human clinical benefit.

concerns.issue: Median human RCT sample size is 20, with concentration in tiny trials
concerns.detail: Among human RCTs with reported sample size, the median is 20 (range 12–81 for gut/digestion). Five of six human studies in gut/digestion fall at or below n=20. A single outlier (n=81) could substantially shift perceived effect direction if pooled; conversely, systematic bias in a small trial (e.g., differential dropout, unblinded assessment) could dominate the average. Mood's n=423 trial is an exception, but it stands alone.

appraisal.mechanism_check: The proposed mechanism—that L. rhamnosus modulates gut microbiota composition and butyrate-producing strains, which then improves barrier function, immune tolerance, and systemic mood—is biologically plausible and the in vitro and animal literature supports microbial metabolite production. However, the leap from microbial composition change (evident in some trials) to clinical outcomes (e.g., postoperative recovery, depression symptoms, skin appearance) is large. The studies do not consistently measure the proposed intermediates (butyrate, barrier integrity, immune markers) in concert with clinical endpoints, so it is unclear whether the organism's effects on clinical outcomes, if real, proceed via the stated mechanism or via unrelated pathways.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would note that (1) no outcome has replication across independent human studies; (2) most positive signals come from n=20 RCTs, which are underpowered to detect modest effects and highly susceptible to bias; (3) the mood trial (n=423) is a single, large, non-replicated study and could easily be a false positive; and (4) the absence of a pooled effect estimate means the 'Moderate' grade is not anchored to a quantified magnitude of benefit. The compound may have no clinically meaningful effect, and the appearance of signal may reflect publication bias, selective outcome reporting, or chance clustering in small trials.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A pre-registered, adequately powered (n≥200) RCT in a single clinical population (e.g., postoperative infection prevention, or depressive symptoms in pregnancy) with blind randomization, allocation concealment, low attrition, pre-specified primary endpoints, and transparent reporting of all measured outcomes would either confirm or refute the signal. Additionally, a systematic meta-analysis with published protocols (PROSPERO) synthesizing all identified human RCTs and reporting heterogeneity, publication bias, and sensitivity analyses would clarify whether effects are robust or an artifact of small-study bias.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Bacteria benéfica viva que se encuentra naturalmente en alimentos fermentados y el intestino humano.
explanation_es.what_it_is: Lactobacillus rhamnosus es un microorganismo vivo —un tipo de bacteria— que ocurre naturalmente en alimentos fermentados como yogur y kéfir, y coloniza el tracto digestivo humano. Pertenece a una clase llamada bacterias del ácido láctico, que producen ácido láctico como subproducto del metabolismo. Las personas típicamente la consumen como suplemento probiótico en forma de cápsula, polvo o alimento fermentado, suministrando células vivas destinadas a sobrevivir el estómago y establecerse en el colon.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Se establece en el intestino y produce compuestos que moldean la digestión, la función de barrera y la señalización inmunitaria.
explanation_es.how_it_works: Cuando se ingiere, las células de Lactobacillus rhamnosus viajan por el tracto digestivo y colonizan el colon. Una vez allí, producen ácido láctico y otros metabolitos (moléculas producidas por células vivas) que reducen el pH, haciendo el colon menos hospitalario para bacterias dañinas. Las bacterias también producen ácidos grasos de cadena corta —especialmente butirato, un combustible clave para las células del colon— que fortalecen la barrera intestinal (la pared selectiva que permite que entren nutrientes pero bloquea toxinas). Además, las células bacterianas interactúan con sensores inmunitarios que recubren el intestino, desencadenando señales que modulan la respuesta inflamatoria del sistema inmunitario. Estos mecanismos en conjunto influyen en la absorción de nutrientes, la integridad intestinal y la tolerancia inmunitaria, por lo que se estudia en condiciones que van desde la recuperación digestiva hasta resultados relacionados con el estado de ánimo.
explanation_es.safety_line: La mayoría de ensayos reportaron pocos efectos secundarios; la seguridad a largo plazo y los grupos específicos en riesgo permanecen poco estudiados.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos humanos recuperados entre 2008–2023 generalmente reportaron tolerabilidad sin eventos adversos mayores en las poblaciones probadas (grupos pequeños, duraciones cortas: típicamente semanas a algunos meses). Sin embargo, estos estudios se realizaron en poblaciones estrechas —principalmente adultos inmunocompetentes y niños en entornos clínicos específicos (recuperación posoperatoria, síndrome de intestino corto, alergia alimentaria). Los datos de seguridad a largo plazo y los efectos en individuos vulnerables o inmunocomprometidos no están representados en los registros proporcionados.
safety_bullets: Individuos inmunocomprometidos (VIH/SIDA, trasplante de órganos, quimioterapia): casi todos los ensayos excluyeron estas poblaciones; la efectividad y seguridad no se han probado en estos grupos.
Síndrome de intestino corto severo o enfermedad crítica: evidencia limitada; un pequeño ensayo (n=12, 2008) lo probó pero la generalización es poco clara.
Interacciones farmacológicas: ningún ensayo recuperado examinó interacciones con antibióticos o inmunosupresores; el momento de coadministración y la eficacia son desconocidos.
Embarazo y lactancia: un ensayo (n=423, 2017) abordó el estado de ánimo posparto; la seguridad durante el embarazo mismo no se detalla explícitamente en los registros.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: Lactobacillus rhamnosus es una célula viva grande y compleja más que una pequeña molécula química. Sus efectos terapéuticos dependen de su viabilidad (si las células están vivas) y su capacidad de sobrevivir el ácido estomacal y llegar al colon intactas. Las formulaciones probióticas a menudo incluyen recubrimientos protectores o se administran en cápsulas entéricas diseñadas para resistir el ácido estomacal, permitiendo que las células lleguen al intestino donde pueden establecerse y metabolizar.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seis ensayos humanos aleatorizados (2008–2023, muestra total verificada ~153 entre cinco estudios que reportan números de participantes) examinaron resultados digestivos: permeabilidad intestinal y función de barrera en síndrome de intestino corto (n=12, 2008), recuperación posoperatoria después de cirugía pancreática (n=20, 2021), colonización intestinal en recién nacidos prematuros (2023, RCT), y expansión de cepas bacterianas productoras de butirato en lactantes alérgicos a alimentos en fórmula suplementada con probióticos (n=20, 2016). Nueve estudios en animales exploraron mecanismos de fortalecimiento de barrera y balance microbiano. En conjunto, los datos sugieren beneficios para la integridad de la barrera intestinal y la composición microbiana, aunque los ensayos individuales muestran tamaños de efecto variantes y diseños heterogéneos (poblaciones diferentes, dosis y medidas de resultado).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Existen múltiples RCTs humanos, pero el análisis agrupado está ausente y las poblaciones de estudio difieren sustancialmente (lactantes prematuros, adultos posoperatorios, niños con alergia alimentaria, síndrome de intestino corto), limitando la certeza de un efecto consistente. Los tamaños de muestra son pequeños y la mayoría de resúmenes omiten números de participantes, reduciendo la precisión.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Dos RCTs humanos (n=20 cada uno, 2011 y 2021) midieron biomarcadores inmunitarios (inmunidad humoral, respuesta inmunitaria posoperatoria) y encontraron asociaciones con la administración de Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG. Tres estudios en animales (2018–2026) demostraron modulación inmunitaria —mitigación de características tipo autoinmune, mejora de la respuesta a infección bacteriana y resistencia mejorada a desafío patógeno. Los mecanismos implicaban señalización inmunitaria vinculada al intestino y reducción de carga patógena, sugiriendo que la bacteria influye tanto en el tono inmunitario local como sistémico.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo dos pequeños estudios humanos; muestra total verificada ~40 participantes. Los datos en animales son de apoyo pero no confirman directamente la traslación humana. Sin análisis agrupado humano; los resultados inmunitarios heterogéneos y medidas entre ensayos previenen conclusión firme de un efecto inmunitario universal.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un RCT humano (n=20, 2011) midió microbiota de la piel y biomarcadores inmunitarios humorales en relación con la administración oral de Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG. Un estudio en animales (2024) examinó cómo la bacteria mitigó lesión intestinal inducida por radiación, con efectos indirectos en el tono inmunitario que *podrían* influir en la salud de la piel, aunque resultados de piel no se midieron directamente. Ningún ensayo clínico evaluó directamente la apariencia de la piel o condiciones dermatológicas en humanos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo un ensayo humano con medidas relevantes a la piel; ningún estudio humano independiente replica el hallazgo. Muestra total ~20 participantes. El único estudio humano midió cambios en microbiota y biomarcadores inmunitarios, no resultados clínicos de piel. Evidencia insuficiente para calificar como Moderada; designada como Emergente pendiente de más datos humanos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un RCT grande (n=423, 2017) probó la suplementación con Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001 durante el embarazo y midió síntomas depresivos y de ansiedad posparto. El ensayo examinó una cepa específica (HN001) en una ventana específica (embarazo) y evaluó el estado de ánimo en el período posparto, encontrando asociaciones entre la administración de probióticos y puntuaciones de síntomas reducidas. Ningún estudio en animales abordó directamente el estado de ánimo.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Un único ensayo humano bien potenciado (n=423) con resultado de estado de ánimo claro apoya la calificación Moderada; sin embargo, es el *único* estudio humano en este resultado, por lo que la consistencia entre estudios independientes no puede evaluarse. La generalización más allá del período periparto y otras cepas de Lactobacillus rhamnosus permanece desconocida.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La base de evidencia comprende 15 estudios totales: 10 humanos (principalmente RCTs pequeños, 2008–2023) y 5 ensayos en animales (2018–2026). Los estudios humanos se concentran en recuperación quirúrgica, condiciones pediátricas (síndrome de intestino corto, alergia alimentaria, prematuridad), y un gran ensayo de salud mental periparto. Los estudios en animales exploraron mecanismos inmunitarios y modelos de infección. La diversidad de poblaciones humanas y medidas de resultado, combinada con tamaños de muestra pequeños en la mayoría de ensayos digestivos e inmunitarios, limita la certeza; el único gran ensayo de estado de ánimo (n=423) es el estudio individual más fuerte pero se mantiene solo. En general, el nivel es Moderado, reflejando efectos humanos plausibles apoyados por múltiples ensayos pequeños y datos mecanísticos coherentes en animales, pero limitados por imprecisión y heterogeneidad.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros recuperados muestran brechas en varias poblaciones: individuos inmunocomprometidos, mujeres embarazadas (aparte del ensayo de estado de ánimo de 2017), adolescentes y ancianos están ampliamente ausentes. La mayoría de ensayos son de corto plazo (semanas a algunos meses); la colonización a largo plazo y los efectos persistentes no se han explorado. Para la apariencia de la piel, solo un estudio humano está representado, y midió marcadores, no resultados clínicos. Los registros proporcionados incluyen aproximadamente 40 resúmenes por resultado; esto es una muestra, no la literatura completa, por lo que las afirmaciones sobre brechas en el *campo* serían infundadas —pero estas brechas son visibles en los datos suministrados.

appraisal_es.headline: La base de evidencia descansa en un pequeño número de ensayos con poder estadístico insuficiente sin síntesis metaanalítica; la mayoría de los resúmenes recuperados omiten tamaños de muestra, y ningún resultado tiene replicación independiente convincente en múltiples estudios en humanos.

concerns.issue: Déficit grave de replicación entre resultados
concerns.detail: Gut/digestión tiene solo 6 estudios en humanos (5 ECA, 1 ensayo clínico); función inmunológica tiene 2 ECA en humanos (n=20 cada uno); piel tiene 1 ECA en humanos (n=20); estado de ánimo tiene 1 ECA en humanos (n=423). Solo el estado de ánimo descansa en un único ensayo de tamaño razonablemente grande. Ningún resultado tiene ≥3 ECA en humanos independientes que reporten el mismo punto final clínico, lo que hace imposible evaluar si los efectos se replican o son impulsados por sesgo, heterogeneidad poblacional o azar.

concerns.issue: La mayoría de los estudios recuperados no reportan tamaños de muestra
concerns.detail: El motor señala que 'la mayoría de los resúmenes omiten el tamaño de muestra, por lo que el total verdadero es sustancialmente mayor'—pero esta falta de transparencia significa que el tamaño de muestra efectivo y la precisión del cuerpo general son desconocidos a partir de los registros proporcionados. Para función inmunológica, solo 2 de 5 estudios reportan n; para piel, solo 1 de 2; para estado de ánimo, 1 de 1. La magnitud real de la base de evidencia no puede evaluarse sin esta información, y el reporte selectivo del tamaño de muestra es una señal de alerta de sesgo de publicación.

concerns.issue: Sin síntesis cuantitativa agrupada a pesar de calificación 'Moderada'
concerns.detail: Los cuatro resultados se califican como Moderados o superiores, pero el motor explícitamente establece 'efecto agrupado: ninguno extraíble' para cada resultado. Esto significa que no se realizó metanálisis; las calificaciones reflejan consenso cualitativo sobre tipos de estudios y consistencia aproximada, no una estimación cuantificada del efecto. Una calificación Moderada en evidencia no sintetizada es difícil de calibrar—podría reflejar una señal genuina o simplemente ausencia de contradicciones obvias.

concerns.issue: Confusión de diseño de estudio con área de resultado
concerns.detail: Gut/digestión incluye 9 estudios en animales de 15 totales (60% animales), mientras que función inmunológica, piel y estado de ánimo están fuertemente sesgados hacia ensayos humanos más pequeños o únicos. Esta heterogeneidad en composición de diseño por resultado hace que la comparación entre resultados sea poco confiable. Los modelos animales de digestión pueden no traducirse en beneficio clínico humano.

concerns.issue: La mediana del tamaño de muestra de ECA en humanos es 20, con concentración en ensayos muy pequeños
concerns.detail: Entre ECA en humanos con tamaño de muestra reportado, la mediana es 20 (rango 12–81 para gut/digestión). Cinco de los seis estudios en humanos en gut/digestión se encuentran en o por debajo de n=20. Un único valor atípico (n=81) podría cambiar sustancialmente la dirección del efecto percibido si se agrupara; inversamente, el sesgo sistemático en un ensayo pequeño (p. ej., deserción diferencial, evaluación no ciega) podría dominar el promedio. El ensayo de estado de ánimo n=423 es una excepción, pero permanece aislado.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El mecanismo propuesto—que L. rhamnosus modula la composición de la microbiota intestinal y las cepas productoras de butirato, que luego mejoran la función de barrera, la tolerancia inmunológica y el estado de ánimo sistémico—es biológicamente plausible y la literatura in vitro y en animales respalda la producción de metabolitos microbianos. Sin embargo, el salto desde el cambio en composición microbiana (evidente en algunos ensayos) a resultados clínicos (p. ej., recuperación postoperatoria, síntomas de depresión, apariencia de la piel) es grande. Los estudios no miden consistentemente los intermediarios propuestos (butirato, integridad de barrera, marcadores inmunológicos) en concierto con puntos finales clínicos, por lo que es poco claro si los efectos del organismo en resultados clínicos, si son reales, proceden mediante el mecanismo establecido o mediante vías no relacionadas.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico señalaría que (1) ningún resultado tiene replicación entre estudios independientes en humanos; (2) la mayoría de señales positivas provienen de ECA con n=20, que tienen poder insuficiente para detectar efectos modestos y son altamente susceptibles al sesgo; (3) el ensayo de estado de ánimo (n=423) es un único estudio grande no replicado y fácilmente podría ser un falso positivo; y (4) la ausencia de una estimación de efecto agrupado significa que la calificación 'Moderada' no está anclada a una magnitud cuantificada de beneficio. El compuesto puede no tener efecto clínicamente significativo, y la apariencia de señal puede reflejar sesgo de publicación, reporte selectivo de resultados, o agrupamiento por azar en ensayos pequeños.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un ECA preregistrado, con poder adecuado (n≥200) en una única población clínica (p. ej., prevención de infección postoperatoria, o síntomas depresivos en embarazo) con aleatorización ciega, ocultamiento de asignación, baja deserción, puntos finales prespecificados y reporte transparente de todos los resultados medidos, confirmaría o refutaría la señal. Además, un metanálisis sistemático con protocolos publicados (PROSPERO) sintetizando todos los ECA en humanos identificados y reportando heterogeneidad, sesgo de publicación y análisis de sensibilidad aclararía si los efectos son robustos o un artefacto del sesgo de estudios pequeños.
